summary: This district was built on sand, and in December 1914 the city measured how much: test holes bored across it found bedrock 343 feet down between Santiago and Taraval, 348 feet between Fulton and Cabrillo, 398 feet between Wawona and Yorba. The first streets were redwood curbs and broken rock; the sewers in the lower Sunset had to be buried under fill to hold them up; and in 1923 the Board set aside $900 simply to shift a sand drift off Irving Street. Around that work were sixty horses in a corral between Twentieth and Twenty-first avenues, a well being drilled, and the Great Highway paved a half-width at a time. The avenues then came in one crossing at a time for forty years, with the same contractors asking for another ninety days. Schools followed the houses — the Jefferson School ordered at Nineteenth Avenue and Irving Street in 1920, an annex to the Parkside School in 1925, additions to Francis Scott Key — and in 1931 the Board ordered lighting standards the whole way along Sloat Boulevard, from Nineteenth Avenue to the ocean beach. Lately the Board has been naming what stands out here — the Trocadero Clubhouse in Stern Grove in 2021, the Mother's Building at the Zoo in 2022, the Parkside Branch Library in McCoppin Square in 2023 — and buying whole buildings for affordable housing, on Irving Street and on the Great Highway. In 2023 it closed the Great Highway Extension south of Sloat Boulevard, three thousand three hundred feet of it. And in 2013 the city recorded that the seven-foot dachshund's head was back in place at Sloat Boulevard and Forty-fifth Avenue, with a street party to mark it.
